slides.headline: The hotel was real. The speakers were real people.
slides.sub: Tickets from 149 dollars. Sponsorships up to 25,000.

slides.title:
They did not copy
an event. They
invented one.
slides.body: Proofpoint traced a fake conference called BioTold 2026, advertised for early November at a real Boston hotel. The hotel confirmed it had never heard of it.

slides.title:
Real names did
the convincing.
slides.body: The site listed a Harvard geneticist and a Nobel laureate as speakers, and carried the logos of three well known science companies as sponsors. None of them had agreed to anything.

slides.title:
The payload came
after you replied.
slides.body: Nothing harmful sat on the website. They invited people to speak or sponsor, waited for interest, then sent a follow up link carrying malware that opens the door for ransomware later.

slides.title:
Flattery is the
attack surface.
slides.body: An invitation to speak does not feel like a threat. It feels like recognition. That is exactly why people click the second email without checking the first.

slides.title:
Two things that
still work.
slides.body:
Call the venue, not the organiser. One question to the hotel ends this in a minute.

If an event lists a speaker you can find online, write to that speaker. Someone invited under a false name wants to know.

slides.title:
Follow for more
like this.
